description: Understand molecular docking, QSAR models, virtual screening, and pharmacophore modeling.

slides.title: Welcome to Computational Drug Design
slides.content:
# Computational Drug Design

Welcome to **Computational Drug Design** (also known as In Silico design)!

## What You Will Learn:
- **Molecular docking** - The digital lock and key
- **QSAR models** - Predicting biology with math
- **Virtual screening** - Testing millions of drugs for free
- **Pharmacophore modeling** - Mapping the perfect drug

Modern drugs are designed on supercomputers long before they are ever synthesized in a test tube.

slides.title: The Old Way
slides.content:
# High-Throughput Screening (HTS)

Historically, pharmaceutical companies found drugs via brute force.

They built massive robotic factories that physically mixed millions of random chemical compounds with a disease target in tiny test tubes to see if anything worked.

This is incredibly slow, costs hundreds of millions of dollars, and wastes vast amounts of toxic chemicals.

slides.title: The In Silico Revolution
slides.content:
# Virtual Screening

**Virtual Screening** replaces the robots and test tubes with supercomputers.

If we know the exact 3D shape of a cancer protein (from X-ray crystallography or AlphaFold), we can use a computer to digitally "test" millions of chemical structures to see which ones fit into the protein's active site.

It costs almost nothing, generates no chemical waste, and can screen billions of compounds in weeks!

slides.title: Molecular Docking
slides.content:
# Molecular Docking

The core software used in virtual screening is a **Docking Algorithm**.

## The Goal:
The software attempts to take a small drug molecule (the ligand) and mathematically fit it into the pocket of the large protein target.

It rotates and twists the drug millions of times, trying every possible angle to find the perfect geometric fit.

slides.title: Scoring Functions
slides.content:
# Scoring Functions

Geometry isn't enough; the physics must match.

Once the computer finds a geometric fit, it runs a **Scoring Function**. This is a complex math equation that calculates the thermodynamics of the interaction.

It adds points for good things (hydrogen bonds, opposite electrical charges attracting) and subtracts points for bad things (atoms crashing into each other, like-charges repelling). The best score wins!

slides.title: Virtual Screening Quiz
slides.content: Test your knowledge of computational methods.
slides.quizQuestion: What is the primary advantage of Virtual Screening over traditional High-Throughput Screening?
quizOptions: Virtual screening produces physical pills instantly
Virtual screening requires no computer power
Virtual screening can evaluate millions of compounds cheaply and quickly without needing physical chemicals or robots
Virtual screening only works for viral infections

slides.title: Rigid vs Flexible Docking
slides.content:
# The Complexity Problem

## Rigid Docking:
Early software treated the protein as a solid block of stone. This is fast, but inaccurate, because proteins actually move and breathe (Induced Fit).

## Flexible Docking:
Modern software allows the protein's amino acids to wiggle and shift as the drug enters. This requires exponentially more math and supercomputer time, but drastically increases the accuracy of the predictions.

slides.title: Pharmacophore Modeling
slides.content:
# Pharmacophore Modeling

What if we *don't* know the 3D shape of the target protein?

We can use **Pharmacophore Modeling**. If we already know 5 different drugs that successfully bind to the mystery protein, we align their 3D structures on a computer.

We look for the common features they all share (e.g., "They all have a positive charge here, and a hydrogen bond there"). This abstract 3D map of necessary features is the Pharmacophore.

slides.title: Using the Pharmacophore
slides.content:
# Finding New Drugs

Once you have the 3D Pharmacophore map, you tell the computer:

"Search our database of a billion chemicals. Ignore what they look like, just find me entirely new chemicals that place a positive charge exactly here, and a hydrogen bond exactly there."

This is a powerful way to invent brand new classes of drugs that bypass existing patents!

slides.title: QSAR Models
slides.content:
# QSAR

**Quantitative Structure-Activity Relationship (QSAR)**.

This is the ultimate application of machine learning in drug design. It attempts to predict how powerful a drug will be using only mathematical statistics, without doing any physical docking!

slides.title: Molecular Descriptors
slides.content:
# Teaching the AI

To build a QSAR model, you turn a chemical structure into a list of numbers called **Descriptors**.

- How much does it weigh?
- How fat-soluble is it?
- How many oxygen atoms does it have?
- What is its surface area?

You feed these numbers (for thousands of known drugs) into an AI, along with their known biological activity.

slides.title: QSAR Quiz
slides.content: Verify your understanding of predictive modeling.
slides.quizQuestion: What is the primary goal of a QSAR model?
quizOptions: To simulate the physical docking of a drug into a protein pocket
To use statistical math to predict a chemical's biological activity based solely on its numerical properties (descriptors)
To synthesize chemicals in a robotic lab
To determine the half-life of a drug in a human patient

slides.title: Predicting the Unknown
slides.content:
# The Power of QSAR

The AI finds hidden mathematical correlations (e.g., "Every time the fat-solubility goes up by 1 unit, the drug gets 10 times stronger").

Now, you can draw a brand new chemical that has never existed in reality. The AI will instantly calculate its descriptors and mathematically predict exactly how strong the drug will be, before a chemist ever wastes time synthesizing it!

slides.title: Lipinski's Rule of 5
slides.content:
# Predicting Pharmacokinetics

Computers don't just predict if a drug will bind; they predict if it will survive the human stomach!

**Lipinski's Rule of 5** is a famous algorithm. It states an oral drug will likely be absorbed if:
1. It has less than 5 hydrogen bond donors.
2. It has less than 10 hydrogen bond acceptors.
3. Its molecular weight is under 500.
4. Its fat-solubility score (LogP) is under 5.

slides.title: Filtering the Garbage
slides.content:
# Saving Money

Before a pharmaceutical company runs a massive virtual screen of 100 million compounds, they run them all through Lipinski's Rule of 5.

The computer instantly deletes 90 million compounds that would never survive the human digestive tract.

By filtering the garbage early, they focus all their expensive computing power on drugs that actually have a chance of becoming a daily pill!

slides.title: Summary of Computational Design
slides.content:
# Computational Summary

## Key Takeaways:
- **Virtual Screening** uses computers instead of robots to cheaply test millions of compounds.
- **Molecular Docking** uses geometry and **Scoring Functions** to see if a drug fits a target.
- **Pharmacophores** map the 3D features needed for binding when the target's shape is unknown.
- **QSAR** uses machine learning and descriptors to predict drug activity.
- Algorithms like **Lipinski's Rule of 5** predict if a drug can actually be absorbed by the human body.

slides.title: Course Complete
slides.content:
# Congratulations!

You have completed the Drug Design (MSc) course.

You now understand the incredibly complex journey of how a modern medicine goes from a digital concept to a life-saving pill.
